I ran `up_plan` (the dry-run pre-flight — no provider calls, nothing written). Here's what `kapi up` would do:

## The project
`kapi.yaml` defines one project, **northwind**: a single collection `app` in `src/locales`, source `en.json` → target `{lang}.json`, with `en` → `nb` (Norwegian Bokmål) as the only language pair.

## The plan

| Collection | Locale | Missing target | Content-memory hits | AI units | Est. tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| app | nb | 5 | 0 | 5 | ~22 |

All five strings in `src/locales/en.json` — `greeting`, `intro`, `save`, `cancel`, `settings` — are untranslated, and there's no `nb.json` yet. Content memory has zero exact-hash hits, so nothing gets reused; the full set goes to AI translation via the default built-in flow. The estimate is tiny (~22 tokens, computed as source chars ÷ 4 — no tokenizer involved).

## What that means in practice
`kapi up` would translate all 5 units to Norwegian, run the project's bound checks on the results, loop until the `nb` scope is either shippable or parked for a human, and — per the recipe's materialize policy — write `src/locales/nb.json`. The default flow produces drafts, so the output would land as draft units for review rather than as sign-off-ready translations.

Two things worth flagging before you run it:
- **This is a trivially small job.** 5 units, ~22 tokens. No reason to bound it with `passes` or `jobs`.
- **`kapi-config/update-channel` is set to `beta`.** Not something `up` acts on, but worth knowing you're on the beta channel if behavior surprises you.

Nothing was changed — `up_plan` only reads. Say the word and I'll run the real `up`.
